speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to report to this House with a great deal of pride the selection of the United Nations Peacekeeping Forces as recipient of the 1988 Nobel Peace Prize.
Hear, hear!

I am sure that all Members of the House will join me in expressing their pleasure at this announcement.
This prize has particularly special meaning for Canada. For many years peacekeeping has been accorded a prominent place in Canadian foreign and defence policy.
This Government has made peace and security one of the basic objectives which have framed our approach to the formation of Canadian domestic and international policy over the last four years. Indeed, peacekeeping was one of the primary goals identified for the Canadian Forces in the 1987 White Paper on National Defence.
The effective participation of Canadians Forces in virtually every United Nations peacekeeping operation since the Second World War has contributed directly to the easing of tensions in trouble spots around the world. If there is one thing for which Canada is held in high regard it is our support for the United Nations and for its peacekeeping efforts.
Canada has served on 11 separate UN peacekeeping missions from Korea to the Middle East to the Belgian Congo. We have participated in eight different U.N. truce supervisory or observer missions from Kashmir to Yemen to Lebanon. Finally, we have not restricted ourselves to UN operations alone but have also contributed our expertise to four other non-UN multilateral peacekeeping operations.
Our record is a proud one. Today, almost 2,000 Canadian Forces personnel serve around the world in a score of countries furthering international peace and goodwill. I have in the past indicated in this House and elsewhere that these dedicated officers and enlisted personnel deserve the unqualified support of all Canadians. Polls have indicated that most Canadians do indeed share this point of view.
Peacekeeping has long deserved the type of international recognition and support which today's Nobel Peace Prize announcement embodies. The UN's peacekeeping efforts in the past 40 years have finally received their just recognition, as have those nations, such as Canada, which have actively supported and contributed to such efforts.
Peacekeeping has a special place in Canadian hearts. I think I can say that we invented peacekeeping. Or, rather, the late Prime Minister Pearson invented peacekeeping. For his pivotal role in seeking the peaceful resolution of the Arab-Israeli conflict of 1956 Mr. Pearson was justifiably awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
Today's announcement is a second Nobel Prize involving Canada and its peacekeeping efforts. I join all Canadians in extending our congratulations and our best wishes to our peacekeeping forces around the world. Their job is difficult and dangerous. But their dedication over decades has done much to further the cause of peace in the world.

September 29, 1988
Statements by Ministers

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the Official Opposition to say how pleased we are to see that the Nobel Prize Committee has awarded this year's Peace Prize to UN peacekeepers.
[DOT] (M10)
Canada plays a special role when it comes to the concept of peacekeeping. I think it is clear-and history records this- that this very concept was something created by a Canadian. The late Right Hon. Lester Pearson, when he was Secretary of State for External Affairs in the Government of Louis St. Laurent, at that time convinced the United Nations to establish a force made up of troops of member countries, including Canada, in a way which resolved the Suez crisis of 1956. As a result, Mike Pearson received the Nobel Prize for Peace in 1957.
It occurred to me that it might be said that the awarding of this year's Nobel Prize for Peace to UN peacekeepers is almost like the award of a second Nobel Prize to Mike Pearson, because the award announced today is a confirmation of how important, how valid, and how successful the concept that Mike Pearson developed in 1956 has proven to be over the years.
This award is a tribute, certainly, to the troops of the member countries who have participated and are participating in UN peacekeeping operations around the world, and Canadians have proudly played a leading role in all such forces since their inception. They played an important role with the force created to resolve the Suez crisis, and they are playing an important role today in maintaining the truce which has ended the gulf war between Iran and Iraq.
This award is indirectly a tribute to the Secretary General of the United Nations, Javier Perez de Cuellar and his staff, for their work in bringing about the truce in the gulf war and generally in doing more than has been done for quite a few years in advancing the role of the United Nations in resolving conflicts and preventing them from breaking out into world wars of a scope which has caused such destruction all too often in the past hundred years.
If this award is a tribute to the Secretary General of the United Nations, it is also in recognition of the importance of the United Nations itself in helping to maintain an atmosphere of peace and security in the world. I know that all Canadians are very pleased to find that the peacekeepers of the United Nations have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize.
This is not the first time that UN agencies have been awarded the Nobel Prize, but certainly, because of the role of a Canadian, Mike Pearson, in creating the concept of peacekeeping by the UN, and also because of the role of Canadian troops in all United Nations peacekeeping operations, Canadians, I am sure take great satisfaction in this year's Nobel Prize for Peace.
I conclude by again stating how delighted we are in the Official Opposition that this award has been given to the
Peacekeeping Forces of the United Nations, and I am sure that all Canadians are delighted in the same way and extend their warm congratulations to all those participating in United Nations peacekeeping operations, the forces of Canada and the forces of the many other member nations of the United Nations who are doing so much to justify this Nobel Prize for Peace.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, I would like to join with the Minister and the spokesman for the Official Opposition in congratulating the United Nations Peacekeeping Forces on being recipients of this year's Nobel Peace Prize. I think it is particularly appropriate when we know that over the years this Nobel Peace Prize tends to go to individuals, which is understandable. But the fact remains that over those same years there have been many, many individuals unrecognized in this special way who have been keeping the peace on the ground, where it counts.
We know that over-all, between 1947 and 1988, more than 80,000 Canadian servicemen and servicewomen have participated in 15 peace-restoring, peacekeeping, and truce supervisory operations mounted by the United Nations, and in three truce supervisory or observer missions conducted outside the UN framework.
In 1988, this very year alone, over 1,400 Canadian Forces personnel participated in international peacekeeping forces and observer missions. I am also told that since Korea 79 Canadians have died while serving in peacekeeping forces, something which many Canadians may not know.
What we are recognizing or what has been recognized today in the awarding of this Nobel Peace Prize is the terribly significant and sometimes dangerous role that many Canadians have played, as I said before, on the ground or on the line, literally, in some cases.
I had the opportunity to visit the Green Line in Nicosia, as I am sure the Ministers have had the opportunity to do so, and on a day-to-day basis Canadians there are put in a position where they sometimes have to confront people who are threatening or actually moving into territory that they should not be moving into, and these Canadians put themselves in a very vulnerable position.
That is the kind of real peacekeeping we are recognizing here today. I can say, as has been indicated by previous comments, that the peacekeeping role that Canada has played all these years is something that all Canadians agree on and with. We may disagree with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) on nuclear submarines and on first-use policy of NATO or Cruise missile testing, or whatever the case may be, but I think there is consensus on Canadian defence and foreign policy on the role of the Canadian Armed Forces and being available to the world for these kinds of peacekeeping operations.
September 29, 1988

We need to ask ourselves, 1 suppose, the larger question of how we keep the peace, not just between smaller countries who are fighting but between the superpowers, and that is where the debate enjoins with the Government.
For the moment, let us all come together and rejoice in the fact that the work that many Canadian men and women have done over the years in peacekeeping operations has been duly and honourably recognized.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure to speak on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Jelinek) to address third reading of this Bill, which is important, and I believe all Members agree is important to the unemployed in the weeks and months ahead during the coming year.
During second reading debate and Committee of the Whole stage, Members expressed concern about some areas of unemployment insurance, and that has certainly been taken into consideration. It is for this reason that the Minister of State has asked for a comprehensive review of economic regions so that we can correct some of the things that are wrong with unemployment insurance with respect to the variable entrance requirement. This is the first time that it has been done in 12 years, and it is highly necessary to do so.
September 29, 1988

The unemployment insurance program plays an important role in our social security system. Unemployment insurance benefits replace lost income. They help maintain the stability of local economies, and also help to protect the jobs of people employed in most communities. Bill C-158 contains an extension to the variable entrance requirement from January 4, 1989, to January 6, 1990, to allow the unemployment insurance program to continue to respond to regional differences for the next 12 months. We do not want to create hardship. The extension of the VER will be tangible demonstration that Parliament recognizes the difficulties many Canadians face in finding work.
If the VER is not extended, up to 80,000 recipients in high unemployment regions could find themselves without work, without pay, and unable to meet the eligibility requirements for unemployment insurance benefits.
I am asking the House to approve this amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to maintain the status quo until we have the results of the comprehensive review of economic regions. We will not make changes to this important social program in a haphazard manner. If, when the review is completed, we will feel it is appropriate to make changes, we will come before the House with a detailed plan for the future. It may be that we find the VER, or some variant thereof, to be the best possible way to deal with regional differences, but let us await the evidence.
For the immediate future, unemployment insurance applicants must be assured of the situation regarding their admissibility. Through failure to extend the VER, we do not want anyone to find himself or herself in financial difficulty. Therefore, I ask for the support of all Members of the House that Bill C-158 may be passed with the minimum delay.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to Bill C-158, which is an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to extend the variable entrance requirement. As the Parliamentary Secretary said earlier, the VER has been used for a number of years to maintain the ten-week eligibility period.
Mr. Speaker, although the Bill will maintain the current system and will, in certain cases, be beneficial to Canadian workers, it will do nothing at all for the people of New Brunswick, especially those in the southeast and the entire southern part who are affected by the variable requirement.
In June, the eligibility period for our workers went up to sixteen weeks, in July it went back to ten weeks and then went back up to sixteen weeks in August, where it is now, in September.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
What happened? When Statistics Canada does its surveys to determine the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate in southern New Brunswick, it does about 700 individual surveys, that is, 400 in the Moncton urban region and about 300 in the rural region.
According to these surveys, the unemployment rate in the city of Moncton is very low, and in rural areas it is very high. This means that when both rates are combined and seasonally adjusted, the average rate for the last three months drops below 11.5 per cent, which requires a change in the eligibility period.
The section we propose to change will do nothing for the people of New Brunswick. There are several sections in the Unemployment Insurance Act that have an impact on eligibility. These include Section 17(6), the section we are amending today, and also Section 17(5) and Section 35.
Under these provisions eligibility for and entitlement to UI benefits are determined by three-month average of seasonally-adjusted unemployment rates for the UI economic region in which the UI claimant resides. These unemployment rate estimates are provided monthly by Statistics Canada as a by-product of the Labour Force Survey.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, we are changing only one part, one section, namely 17(6) and not Section 35, which is a shame for the people of New Brunswick.
When workers experienced the first change in July, many people were taken by surprise. They were relieved when in the following month, the 10 week period was reinstated. Subsequently, however, the eligibility period went back to 16 weeks.
Mr. Speaker, in June I received petitions, letters and any number of telephone calls. The same thing happened in July: telephone calls, petitions, letters and visits. The same thing in September: more calls, more petitions and even more visits and letters. In September however, I detected a note of aggressiveness among the workers affected by this measure.
Why? Mr. Speaker, you must realize that in our region, unemployment insurance represents a considerable adjunct to people's income. The workers felt aggressive towards the Department because it had failed to make certain changes. They felt this way because the Minister had made changes in the regulations to accommodate people in another region. These changes were to take effect as of September 11, 1988. According to the Canada Gazette: Her Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, pursuant to paragraph 58(t) of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, is pleased hereby to approve the amendment made by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission to the Unemployment Insurance Regulations, C.R.C., c. 1576, in accordance with the schedule hereto, effective September 11, 1988.

September 29, 1988
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 The change was made in the Outaouais region:
One of the regions is that of Outaouais (UI economic region 49) comprising the city of Hull and the rural areas in the Gatineau River valley northwest of Ottawa. Unemployment rates for Hull have tended to be substantially lower than those for the rural portion of the Outaouais economic region.
Because of the preponderant influence of Hull in the production of these estimates those for Outaouais tend to understate the difficulty of finding employment in the rural part of the region, with the consequence that UI benefit conditions may be more stringent than economic circumstances warrant.
That is why the people in our region have started to show signs of aggressiveness. In their case, changes in the eligibility period are affecting them adversely, but the Government refuses to take any action. It did in the case of another region, as I just pointed out. People are starting to ask questions. Why weren't the same changes made for New Brunswick? What we have here, Mr. Speaker, is a case of gross injustice.
When we talk about the eligibility period and mention ten weeks, some people say 10 weeks isn't very long. Anybody should be able to find work for 10, 15 or even 20 weeks. Mr. Speaker, if enough work was available in my region or in every region in New Brunswick or every region in Canada, people would prefer to work 20, 25 or 30 weeks or even all year round.
The fact remains that for some workers in New Brunswick, 10 weeks of employment is hard to find. Some occupations and certain types of work are seasonal. Fishermen, for example, are guided by the fishing seasons. If we look at the lobster fishery, which provides employment for most of the people in my constituency and in some other New Brunswick ridings, the fishermen, their assistants and the factory workers are limited to 10 weeks for the simple reason that the fishing season is only 10 weeks. There is no question of extending the season. The resource is just not there to support more fishing.
Not only fishermen and those involved in the fishing industry have difficulty. Thare are also construction and forestry workers. Sixteen weeks of work is very hard, and in some cases impossible, to find. Ten weeks is hard enough.
So how does one explain to the people of New Brunswick that the Government really does not want to listen? It remains insensitive and reading the words of the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary raises some doubts about the Government's sincerity, because this Government has already disappointed New Brunswickers in the past and it is doing so again.
I refer to the words of the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, who last Friday, when he introduced changes on second reading of Bill C-158, said, as reported on page 19558 of Hansard, which I quote:
Unfortunately, in some regions, economic recovery is slower and the rate of unemployment remains higher than the national average. A failure to extend the variable entrance requirement at this time would have serious negative consequences for those regions.
He continues:
One of the priorities of our Government is its desire to help those regions that are experiencing economic difficulty. The VER ...
. . . variable entrance requirement . . .
. . . recognizes that it is more difficult to find and keep a job in a region of
high unemployment. This is, in fact, one of the most important aspects of the
UI program, since it takes into account the labour market conditions in each
region of the country.
And I could go on.
Mr. Speaker, this speech could be used to justify changes to the regulations under section 35. So why not make all the changes to ensure that all workers are treated the same way! How can one explain to the people of New Brunswick that this Government, on the one hand, says that it wants to treat them fairly and, on the other, just ignores them?
How can this Government explain to the people that it will not make the changes required to render justice to New Brunswick workers? The speech of the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Friesen), is meaningless. It did not accommodate all the workers. The speech is further rendered meaningless because government Members last Friday defeated a motion that would have established a fixed period of 10 weeks. The amendment was proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) and defeated by government Members who said they wanted to render justice to all the workers.
We have to question the sincerity of the Government and the Minister. We were assured last week that the Bill would not come before us last week, but that it would come this week instead so we would have enough time to propose amendments enabling us to make it fairer to all the workers of Canada. But, no, the Government last Friday wanted to push the Bill through. Two amendments were proposed and both were defeated. How can we not doubt the sincerity of the Government, Mr. Speaker?
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the Government's approach to this issue is totally unacceptable. The Minister is shirking her responsibility, which is to protect the workers. Her inertia is totally unacceptable.
What I find strange in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is that no other New Brunswicker rose to defend the interests of workers in the province. No Member and no Minister said a word, yet we do have two New Brunswick Conservative Cabinet Ministers in this House. The only Minister who did show some interest in this matter is New Brunswick Labour Minister Mike McKee who came here to Ottawa to confer with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall). Her efforts-or mine, for that matter-were to no avail because the Minister simply said she would study the situation, even after the Forget Commission spent millions of dollars reviewing our unemployment insurance program and after a standing committee of this House produced a report on the same subject.
September 29, 1988

Mr. Speaker, this is a good opportunity to talk about the U1C program. It is very useful to some people because it provides additional income to make ends meet, stabilize the local economy, and ensure at least some standard of living. As I said in my opening remarks, our people would much rather work full time all year for the simple reason that they are hard-working men and women who do not like to remain idle. They would welcome year round employment which would bring in a lot more money than UIC benefits ever do.
Some people maintain that unemployment insurance payments make life too soft for our workers. Mr. Speaker, I object to such comments. Some working couples in New Brunswick are in a situation where the man or the woman earns $6 an hour, 40 hours a week. That brings in $240 a week or, over 50 weeks, an income of something like $12,000 a year. The partner also works 40 hours a week at $4.50 an hour, or $180 a week. If he or she is lucky enough to work for 10 weeks the take-home pay is $1,800. And if subsequently, he is eligible for unemployment insurance, he will get $108 per week for 40 weeks, which will give him another $4,300. This means the couple has to live on $18,100, which is less than our nontaxable allowance here in the House. However, when they buy groceries, they have to pay the same price we do for groceries or for other services.
I think a comparison would be useful. There are people who say we spend too much money on unemployment insurance and that some people take advantage of the system. Recently, I saw all kinds of press releases on my desk announcing grants to various businesses in my region and other regions. There was one grant for $160,000, and that isn't much as government grants go, when you consider that some are for millions of dollars. This was a grant for $160,000 to one individual, to help him set up some kind of building. If we look at the person who gets $4,000 a year, that person would have to be on unemployment insurance for 40 years to get the equivalent of the grant that this individual received in one lump sum. So we shouldn't say we are spoiling people with unemployment insurance. We are just giving them back a certain amount of income that gives them a measure of stability.
Besides, the money spent on the unemployment insurance program is subsequently spent by recipients on food, shelter and clothing. The purpose is to help them meet their basic needs, which in many cases cannot all be met.
What should we do, Mr. Speaker, with this program? Instead of making it more restrictive we should try and expand it. Recently, at the beginning of the academic year in community colleges in New Brunswick, many young people came to my office. They had trouble with unemployment insurance. They had worked and were eligible for unemployment insurance, and they decided that since they were no longer employed and had nothing to do, they would be better off going to college to take a course. However, a number of these young people were not lucky enough to be eligible for a regular manpower program. When they were not selected by the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
Department of Employment and Immigration and decided to continue their education anyway, they were told: Too bad, we are going to cut off your unemployment insurance. So the only option these young people had was to stay home in order to collect unemployment insurance, because if they left home to take a course, they were no longer eligible.
Changes should be made in the program to deal with this kind of situation and to unable young people to continue their education. People often say young people should go back to school to continue their education and learn a trade. In this case, however, when they were willing to do so, they were told: No, stay home and collect unemployment insurance. The program could be expanded and this would be entirely in line with the recommendations of the Standing Committee of the House on Labour, Employment and Immigration.
In the first part of their report, they said, first, that everyone should be treated the same, wherever they live.
[English\
Second, meeting the longer-term needs of employees for stable employment and financial security and of employers for an appropriately trained and educated workforce should be recognized as legitimate objectives for the use of the unemployment insurance program. Third, employers and employees need a simple, intelligible and easily administered program.

And I could go on.
Further on in the Committee's report, they said that the eligibility standard should not be tightened and the level and duration of benefits should not be reduced in regions of high unemployment. They also believe that beneficiaries in all regions should be treated the same way. It was a unanimous report of this Committee, where, of course, all Parties were represented.
We could have taken the opportunity given to us, when changes were proposed to the Unemployment Insurance Act in Bill C-158, to accommodate all workers. We could also have made the changes recommended by the Labour, Employment and Immigration Committee, whose first recommendation was to adopt 10 weeks of insurable employment as a common eligibility standard.
So why was this opportunity not taken? All the arguments are there, all the documentation is there. So why did the Minister choose to study this problem again when all the data to make the decisions are there and especially when we know that some changes have been made to the regulations to accommodate workers in some regions of Canada?
So why refuse to make the changes needed to accommodate New Brunswick workers? That is a question which the Minister and this Government will have to answer for New Brunswickers.

September 29, 1988
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
At the stage we are now, it is impossible or almost impossible to amend the Bill, for the simple reason that the only acceptable amendment would be to refer this Bill to a committee for further review, which would only delay the Bill more.
As 1 said right at the beginning, even though this Bill does not go far enough to accommodate the people of New Brunswick, it must still be passed because it will do some good for some people, some workers.
So, Mr. Speaker, although I support Bill C-158, I ask the House, all Hon. Members and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) to take immediate action to change the Unemployment Insurance Regulations so as to reinstate the 10-week qualifying period.
New Brunswickers demand this justice and they deserve to be treated the same way as all other working men and women, wherever they live in Canada.

He is preaching for a cause here today. He wants me to go easy on the next Bill which is about banks. He recognizes that there will be a new Government sitting on the other side after the election, and he is here preaching for a position. I have decided that he is a good candidate to be the ombudsman for the banking system.
I want to participate in this debate on third reading of Bill C-158, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971. This Bill is better known as the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act, amending the variable entrance requirement. People watching might want to know what the variable entrance requirement is. Back in 1977, under the previous Liberal Government, the variable entrance requirement was introduced into the Unemployment Insurance Act. What it did was to divide the country into 48 economic regions. In order to participate in the unemployment insurance program, an individual who is unemployed and eligible would require a certain number of weeks depending on the unemployment rate in that region. The higher the unemployment rate in the region, the lower the number of weeks required to participate.
For example, an individual living in a region that had 6 per cent unemployment or lower, would require 14 weeks for a renewal claim under the unemployment insurance program. An individual living in a region with between 6 per cent and 7 per cent unemployment, would need 13 weeks. An individual living in a region with between 7 per cent and 8 per cent unemployment, would need 12 weeks. An individual living in a region with 8 per cent to 9 per cent unemployment, would need 11 weeks, and for an individual living in an area of over 9 per cent unemployment, 10 weeks is required. Therefore, if one lives in a region that has a double digit unemployment rate,
only 10 weeks of insurable earnings are required to participate in the unemployment insurance program.
That variable entrance requirement was introduced in 1977, and here we are 11 years later and we still have need for that clause in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
While the New Democratic Party will give quick passage to Bill C-158, I think it is important that we go on record that the solution to the problem is not this temporary clause that was put in the Act in 1977 to recognize regionally disadvantaged areas of the country. We do not see that as the solution. In fact, every single time we have to renew this variable entrance requirement, such as we are doing today in Bill C-158, which will take us to 1990, we are admitting that in this country we have not been able to resolve the problem of regional disparities.
After 11 years, seven of them Liberal and four of them Conservative, we are still unable to deal with the most serious economic problem of this country, regional disparities. We have been unable to spread out economic development in this nation. We are still saying that the solution to regional disparities is to make provisions in our social insurance programs so that areas that are condemned forever to be high unemployment areas will have easier access to our social programs such as unemployment insurance. This is an admission of failure on the part of this Conservative Government, and the Liberal Government also failed. Governments came up with DREE, DRIE, ERDA, 1RDP, FEDNOR, the Atlantic Opportunities Agency, the Western Diversification Fund, a whole host of these things, and we still have need for the variable entrance requirement. In fact, of the 48 economic regions under the unemployment insurance program, 23 require only 10 weeks to be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. Fifty per cent of the 48 regions still have double digit unemployment rates. I think that this is an indictment of failed policies over the last four years of this Conservative Government.
What has been the Government's principal underlying regional development? It is the jail-house principle. If we want to diversify regionally the economy of a community, we put a jail in the community. That is the Government's response. Manicouagan has high unemployment. Individuals there require 10 weeks to participate in the unemployment insurance program. So what the Government does is to put a jail in Manicouagan. We have a problem in Newfoundland with high unemployment. They build a jail there.
It is a sad commentary when we have replaced well thought out regional diversification programs with this jail house principle. It is a sad commentary when communities vie with each other and compete with each other for the sake of getting a jail because that is the way to get 60 more jobs and, with other spin-offs, 100 more jobs. That is a sad, sad commentary of this Government. On the eve of an election, to bring the variable entrance requirement for renewal before Parliament is a sad commentary.
September 29, 1988

What are the hopes for the future? This Government signed the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal and in fact condemned the regions to being forever hewers of wood and drawers of water. In fact, it prevents any direct intervention by a Government with respect to incentives or subsidies or in terms of helping regions to diversify their economies.

speechtext:
It is true, and the Tories are very sensitive about that. It is a clear surrender. The only part of this country that is going to have jobs is the Golden Horseshoe in Ontario. It is significant to note that while the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will get up and blow his horn over the 60 days of the next campaign, talking about how many hundreds of thousands of jobs he has created, the vast majority of those jobs are created within a 60 mile radius of Toronto. Everybody in Canada cannot live in the Metropolitan Toronto region. There are parts of this country, such as the region I come from, the Sudbury basin, which has a right and expectation to economic development.
We are a mining community and we are proud of that tradition. We believe that we have some expertise in hard rock mining. One would think there would be an economic strategy developed that would recognize that here is an area that ought to be a centre for mining technology. Its post-secondary institutions should be developing the kinds of research and development in mining that would allow this country to be in the forefront of such things as the detection of rock bursts. One would have thought the Sudbury basin, which is recognized all over the world as being a leader in the mining of nickel and copper, would be the centre for the development, production and manufacture of mining equipment. The scoop trams on the ground and the robotics that are now infiltrating the mines should be produced in the Sudbury basin. Yet, 70 per cent of the mining equipment used in the mines in the Sudbury basin are imported into this country from Sweden, Finland and West Germany.
After 11 years of attempting to diversify this country regionally we find that the only solution that the Tories have is the continuation of the Liberals' inability to do anything about the problem when they were the Government. Their only answer is to renew the variable entrance requirement, to recognize it, to enshrine it in legislation, and to tell the victims of the lack of the Government's ability to deal with regional disparities that at least things will be made easy for them to get on the unemployment insurance rolls. That is the answer from the Government and it is not good enough.
Is it because they lack the will? No sooner did they win the election in 1984 that in November of 1984 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stood up and made an economic statement. In the economic statement he had something to say about the unemployment insurance program. He did not say that the Government was going to work to eliminate regional disparity so there will not be a need for the variable entrance
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
requirement, so there will not be a need for regional extended benefits, because that is the other little part of this game. The little scam is that if we have a high unemployment, "rate we can extend your benefits beyond the 49 weeks in the Act".
What did they do in the economic statement in 1984? No sooner had they won the election that they said that the retirment benefits, the pensions of all those who take retir-ment, will be considered as earned income. That was a time when in many of the regions the resource companies were having a rough time and were encouraging workers to take early retirment to protect the employment of younger workers. They got caught. They got it coming and going. They were losing their jobs, they took the early retirement, the Government changed the rules, and they lost their UI benefits because the pension was then considered to be earned income.
We on this side of the House objected to that. We asked the Government why it would do that. The Government said that was only the first step, that it was going to hire 800 Keystone Cops that would go across the country and enforce the Unemployment Insurance Act. It was going to get tough with the cheaters. So while, on the one hand, it said it was saving some money by making pension income earned income, it was hiring 800 Keystone Cops to go across the country to get tougher with the unemployed. That is how the Government resolved the problem.
What about the real problems? The Government said it was also going to undertake a study. It set up Mr. Forget with a commission that spent $6 million to study the unemployment insurance program. He came back with such right-wing recommendations that not even this Casper Milquetoast Government could accept those recommendations. Therefore, the Forget Commission report, which cost the taxpayers $6 million, is sitting on a shelf gathering cobwebs.
A standing committee of this House made up of Members from all sides, with a majority of Conservatives, studied the Forget Commission report and came back and said that the variable entrance requirement is basically unfair, that the real problem is regional development. The variable entrance requirement simply institutionalizes the unfairness.
The committee dealt with the issue that if you were unemployed in Toronto, where the unemployment rate is very low, and you are 39 or 42 years of age, and if you are 40 years of age and living in St. John's, Newfoundland, the effect of unemployment is the same. The older worker in southern Ontario who cannot get a job and the worker in Newfoundland who cannot get a job are experiencing the same difficulty. No one is to say that just because he is living in an area where there is low unemployment he should be able to get a job and that the person in Newfoundland will have difficulty getting one because the unemployment rate is high. The effects of unemployment are the same. The feelings of frustration about not being able to get a job because you are an older worker are the same.

September 29, 1988

So the standing committee recommended that, instead of going to a variable entrance requirement, we go to 10 weeks no matter where you are in the country. That recommendation was unanimously approved by Conservative Members, Liberal Members, and the New Democratic Party Members on the committee. The thinking was that if we cannot light a stick of dynamite under the Government to come to grips with regional development and regional disparities as a result of lack of economic development, then maybe we could focus its attention because if the cost in the social insurance program were to be very high then it would have to pay attention to that particular problem.
Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, the standing committee's report is sitting on a shelf on the same level as the Forget Commission report gathering cobwebs and dust. So now, in the Government's dying days, the Minister of State for Employment and Immigration (Mrs. Vezina) said in a press release dated September 16 that she is going to set up a study of the variable entrance requirement. One more time we will go back to this business of studying the variable entrance requirement.
We have studied the unemployment insurance program to death. We have studied the variable entrance requirement and the regional extended benefits program to death. That is not where the problem lies. The problem lies with fulfilling what the Prime Minister promised, which he has not delivered, that is, jobs, jobs, jobs. We are talking about jobs in the regions of this country. When the election is on we are going to remind this Conservative Government that it has failed the people of Canada.
You cannot offer to the people of the regions of the country the sop of a variable entrance requirement. Although it may deal with the present, there is nothing in there that holds hope that things are going to change in the regions and that when we, at great expense, educate our children in those regions they can find jobs in those communities and take their place side by side and help to support the community which gave them their shelter and their education.
I want to say to you and to the people of Canada, Mr. Speaker, that there is hope because there is a Party here on this side of the House, the New Democratic Party, which recognizes the inherent and generic problem. It is not the VER but the question of regional development and of creating employment opportunities for regions in northern Ontario, eastern Canada, northern British Columbia, and right across the country so that when you grow up in a community you are able to take your place in that community when you reach manhood or womanhood.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-140, an Act to amend the Bank Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on June 30, 1988, I had the honour to inform this House of the Government's policy regarding service charges as they apply to personal accounts in financial institutions. I am sure that many Members will recall the positive contribution to this policy development process made by the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.
The committee helped to focus attention on a significant public issue which was created when services were unbundled by financial institutions. Unbundling these services made it possible for the financial community to better tailor and market retail services. It was perhaps fairer to unbundle them than to have the user pay. But I believe that same financial community failed to make it clear to customers that individual services would have charges attached to them.
You know, Mr. Speaker, as a result of this customers had insufficient warning, in my view, that service charges were being imposed. They also had insufficient warning that they were being increased. The public, accustomed to free retail services, was by turn puzzled, then annoyed, and then infuriated and outraged with what was happening.
I know that there are many in the financial community who think that the Government has no place telling business how to operate. However, in this instance there is clear evidence of the need for government action.

While wishing to avoid price regulation, it was the Government's view that this issue could best be resolved by ensuring that the essential conditions for real competition existed. First among these conditions is an informed consumer. To ensure this, the Government adopted notification and disclosure of service charges as the key components of its legislative initiative.
September 29, 1988

In doing so, we wanted to ensure that Canadians would be in a better position to make informed banking decisions and price comparisons. Moreover, we were convinced that free market competition, not government regulation, was the best way to bring about fair pricing practices.
To sustain such a system, it was necessary to require that institutions create and publicize mechanisms for handling consumers' complaints. Moreover, we felt that the Government had a role in monitoring and publishing information about the relative prices of financial services.
To this end, my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), agreed to publish tables comparing the relative costs of such basic services.
This publication will ensure that financial institutions continue to comply with their voluntary undertakings. The first such publication was released on August 31, 1988. [English]
The Superintendent of Financial Institutions has examined actions taken by financial institutions to remove various service charges. His report shows that in almost every case, compliance has been achieved or will be achieved in the very near future. I regret that I cannot use visual aids in the House. I went into my bank this morning where I saw a notice to revise fees, which I asked the bank manager if I could take home as a souvenir. He very kindly gave it to me to bring to the House today. I regret that I cannot table it and show it to the House this morning.
The Superintendent's report shows that in almost every case compliance has now been achieved or will be achieved in the very near future. Bill C-140 was one of two elements in the Government's response to the public's concern. The other elements of that response resulted from individual discussions I had with the major financial institutions in Canada.
The principal outcome of these discussions was the voluntary elimination of certain charges for personal account holders. Furthermore, the institutions acted voluntarily to ensure that basic personal banking services were available at little or no cost, as this display which I cannot show indicates.
As a result, six service charges, which most Canadians found to be objectionable, have been removed by various federal financial institutions. Specifically, recipients of NSF cheques are not charged for depositing such cheques in their personal accounts. There is no charge for closing personal accounts that have been opened for more than 90 days. For basic personal accounts no charges will be levied when the balance falls below a specified minimum. There are no charges now for transactions resulting from the institution's error as opposed to the customer's error. Administration and transfer fees on fixed term deposits, notes and GICs will not be increased during the term of these instruments. Finally, for dormant accounts with balances over $10, customers will be charged only if they have not responded to a letter advising them that a charge could occur.
These are substantive improvements. I am very proud that this Parliament, this Government, has had the influence to
Bank Act
bring this about. Much has been achieved through voluntary action.
However, to complete this initiative legislative action is now required. There are those in the House who would like to legislate everything and have nothing done voluntarily, even though all three Parties, as I noted during the hearings of the committee, were willing to have a voluntary approach to this. We do believe that a great deal has been accomplished through voluntary compliance-as a matter of fact, everything that we wanted to have accomplished. But to complete this initiative some legislative action is now required. Fet me briefly explain what is required and what the major provisions of this legislation are.
Bill C-140 is intended to improve the standards that banks must meet in notifying and disclosing service charges to their personal account holders in Canada. The Bill will also require for the first time ever that banks create and publicize procedures for handling consumer complaints. They are not required now by law to have a procedure. My hon. friend opposite mentioned to me a case this morning in which there is not a complaints procedure in a particular branch. This will be the law of Canada. They will have to have a complaints procedure in place. As a matter of fact, most banks and most branches as well as large trust companies have this procedure already up and running. It will now be required by law as a result of this Bill. These procedures will be submitted to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
When customers open a personal account they will be entitled to receive the following. First, they will receive a copy of the contract to which they have agreed. This was not necessarily the case before. They will receive a list of the service charges applied to the account. When you go in to open an account, Mr. Speaker, or when your son or daughter does, for the first time ever they must not only get a contract to take home but they must have a list of the service charges which will be applied to that account, which is disclosure, the heart of this Bill. Third, they will be given information on how they can expect to be notified of any modifications on the charges must be supplied. Fourth, they will receive information on the bank's procedures for handling complaints, this must be there when you open an account. Right now, this may or may not occur. This will be required as a result of this legislation.
The Bill also requires that banks provide ongoing disclosure of services charges on personal accounts. One cannot make our system work without notification. How can you decide whether you are going to change banks or not, because you do not like the level of service charges, if you do not have adequate notification that the services charges are going to change? We require adequate advance notification of changes. Not everybody gets a statement in the mail, but most personal account holders do. For those who receive statements, this notice must be included with their statement. It must be at least 30 days in advance, that is for all of us who receive statements in the mail, and that is most people.

September 29, 1988
Bank Act
Changes will also be posted at least 60 days in advance in the branches and at banking machines. So if you do not get a statement in the mail, there has to be a notice in the bank or at the banking machines. By the way, that is an improvement on what the committee recommended, that the banking machines as well have changes in fees.
I am very, very proud of this, because this notification will make the system work. This will allow the consumer to shop and to go to the bank manager and say, "I have had enough of these charges. I hear that the trust company or bank across the street does not charge nearly as much for service charges. I am going to change my account". You cannot make that decision if there is not adequate prenotification and adequate disclosure of what fees are.
I respect very much the Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), but when this Bill came forward he said something which was patently untrue, and the Bill has made this clear. That is, in addition to these measures, significant penalties for breach of the disclosure and complaints provisions are also included. The penalties provide for a maximum fine of half a million dollars for a violation of these provisions. These are large fines, they are five, ten times more than what is presently in the Bank Act. The Member for Ottawa-Vanier said there were no penalties. There are penalties, and there are enormous penalties. I hope that he will acknowledge that.
Recently, I announced as well that the Government intends to bring forth some amendments to this Bill, to reach beyond helping personal account holders and to help the small business sector. Although the committee that looked at this piece of legislation did not look at small business, 1 was determined to get our response to the committee, which had to do with individual accounts, personal accounts, in order to get our response on the record. Therefore, we brought out our response.
1 also wanted some time, a few months, to use that as a model for our response for small business. A great many of these principles are equally valid for small business.
Therefore, I notify the House today that the Government intends to bring forward amendments to Bill C-140 which will extend similar notification and disclosure methods to business account holders in Canada.
This package, complete with amendments, and the passage of this legislation will ensure that business has greatly enhanced information about the cost of financial services. Banks will be required to keep a list of all their standard charges for business services. Such lists must be made available to the public for examination, upon request, in bank branches doing commercial business.
If you are a very small business operator, you may not want a list to take home of every conceivable service charge. That could be a very long list for businesses. It should be available to you, either on a computer screen or in the branch in written form, and that is established in this legislation. Such lists must
be made available to the public for examination, upon request, in the branches doing commercial business.
Among other things, this will include the standard charges applying to loans and the standard charges applying to mortgage renewals.
All Members of Parliament get complaints from time to time about charges connected with loans and charges connected with renewing mortgages. These must be spelled out in this list as well. The information will include the information on standard application and search fees and on the cost of wiring funds abroad.
From now on, all the core business account charges must be published in a brochure, which can be taken from the branch. Both corporations and unincorporated businesses, including farmers, will now be able to shop around for the best deal. This core list will be outlined in the regulation.
I have to tell you that these amendments on behalf of the small business community and farmers and unincorporated businesses are made in order to respond to our belief that proper notification and proper pre-notification is essential to making the system work. We are also responding to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and other small business groups who have argued that this is essential. They are very, very pleased with these amendments that we are bringing into the Bill to cover and to help the small business community.
As a result of these changes, when making contractual arrangements, businesses will know the base against which they are negotiating. Those who do not want to negotiate a package will have better information about the cost of their banking services.
I would like to say a word about that. Most businesses actually have a customized arrangement with their banks. They go in and say, "Listen, I am going to be asking for all these bank services during the year. What are you going to charge me for them?" They will quote a number, $2,000 or $3,000, and you will want to compare that with what it would be without having a customized relationship or a contractual relationship that is customized for you in particular.
This will now be possible because all the fees must be made available for those who are not on a customized contract basis in the bank branch, and the small business operator can make that comparison and decide whether it is better to have a customized approach or to pay the standard fees as they occur.

Mr. Speaker, 1 believe that the package of initiatives, both voluntary and legislative, this Government has brought forward amply demonstrates our commitment to ensuring that there is real competition in financial services both at the retail and commercial level. Government monitoring will serve to underpin that competition.
September 29, 1988

Mr. Speaker, this Government believes that real competition, not regulation, is the best means of ensuring that Canadians have access to the broadest spectrum of financial services at the lowest cost. The informed consumer is the key element in real competition. Once the measures 1 have outlined are in place Canadians will be equipped to make better choices and the consequent competition will work to the benefit of all.

Let me conclude with this. I plead with Members on all sides of the House this morning to recognize that if we today can pass this in all stages and in committee stage, we can have a regime in place tomorrow, or close to tomorrow, for consumers, for individuals, and for small business in Canada. Those who hold up this particular Bill-the heart of which, by the way, was agreed to by all three Parties in the standing committee who looked at this question-may be making this impossible.
I plead with Members on all sides of the House-because all sides of the House participated in putting together this solution-to support this Bill. Let us have debate in the Committee of the Whole rather than sending it to a legislative committee. I can answer all the questions there. I can help with answers on regulations pursuant to the Bill. This Bill is one of the more important things that any Government can do for consumers and small business. Let us get it done, and let us get it done quickly.

Some Hon Members: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Therefore, we will proceed on debate. I will recognize a Member from the Official Opposition. The Hon Member for Ottawa-Vanier.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, given the comments made by the Hon. Member from the NDP, I think I should protect our position, and not getting any information from the Government as to whether it will proceed this day, I think I should make my remarks which are pertinent to Bill C-140.
The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), our critic in this area, would have liked to be here this morning. Unfortunately, she cannot, but she will be here this afternoon and possibly will participate in the debate later on.
We now begin the second reading debate of Bill C-140, an Act to amend the Bank Act. As I said previously, it was introduced on June 30, 1988, in response to the report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs dated June 6, 1988, on personal financial service charges. I will provide briefly a background to this sensitive and important issue.
All Members of Parliament have heard from their constituents on the topic of financial service charges for consumers. Complaints and concerns were so omnipresent that the standing committee decided to look into it. On March 29, 1988, a background paper by the committee's research staff was released. It concluded that when financial institutions began to compete for business by paying higher interest rates and providing more services, they imposed fees too quickly and without much sensitivity.
The report stated that, on average, routine financial service charges per family cost about $100 a year. This is not excessive. However, the problems stem from lack of information about them. The committee held public hearings during April to hear from consumer groups, financial institutions, and Government. Our focus was the consumer's need for information and the recent changes in levels and structures of service charges.
On June 6, 1988, the committee tabled its report which called for regulations to provide better information on charges, provide certain basic services without charge, such as low balance accounts often held by children and low-income individuals, and prohibit certain charges altogether. For example, the committee recommended the following fees be prohibited: fees to close an account which has been open for more than one year; and fees levied when customers fail to make transactions on an account. The committee also proposed that penalties for banks that failed to do the above be stiffened, an that the office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions create an internal office to deal with consumer complaints.
September 29, 1988

My Party wholeheartedly concurred in the recommendations of the report. The banks responded defensively. The Canadian Bankers' Association said that the committee's recommendations were "interventionist" and went against the stated free enterprise philosophy of the Government.
On June 23, 1988, the Efon. Member for Trinity spoke to an opposition motion put by the NDP. Strangely, after tabling a minority report, they then moved a motion to support the committee report. The Hon. Member said at the time that neither blatant bank bashing by the NDP, calling for regulation at any cost, nor a staunch Conservative anti-regulation policy were useful in this debate. More careful consideration is required in this matter. She concluded that regulation of financial service charges should be a last resort. Instead of responding defensively, the banks should have admitted they went too far and too fast with their user-pay notion, irritating, confusing and inconveniencing their customers. The whole fiasco was a botched public relations exercise on the part of the banks.
On June 30, 1988, the Government responded to the committee's report in the form of Bill C-140. Earlier that week, five of Canada's six major banks said they would voluntarily comply with the committee's recommendations. The main purpose of the legislation at the time was to assure Canadians that the Government would simply monitor the banks' voluntary compliance. I also expressed my dissatisfaction with the Bill in the House on the same day. I said that the Government caved in to the banks. I called for more specific measures, namely inclusion of time limits in the legislation so Canadian consumers would know when services would be provided that treated them with fairness.
What is the status of the banks' activity in this area? On August 17, 1988, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) tabled the report of the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions regarding compliance by banks with the voluntary measures, and preparation for implementing future measures with respect to bank service charges. The conclusion? As of that date the survey done by the office indicated that four banks, the Royal Bank, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Scotiabank, and the Bank of Montreal appeared to be complying with the letter and spirit of the voluntary measures agreed upon. One bank, the National Bank, reported it was in compliance except for the withdrawal of the NSF charge back fee. This was to be done by November, 1988. Another bank, the Toronto-Dominion, was in compliance except for the provision of a no-frills account.
As a result of this report, a member of the standing committee withdrew his Private Members' Bill that would have legislated the now voluntary measures. Therefore, it appears that voluntary compliance has occurred in large part. Consumers, aware of where it has not occurred, can take their business elsewhere. They can act. They have a choice.
Bank Act
I will now turn my attention to the issue of financial service fees for small businesses. That is an important matter which I do not think was addressed sufficiently. At the time of the tabling of the report on personal financial service charges, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business made its views known. It wanted equal time and fair treatment from the banks. The Minister responded that he wanted small businesses to be treated largely the same as consumers, and that he would change the legislation to ensure this. He announced his intention to do so on September 15, less than two weeks ago.
The CFIB understood that the committee focused on the consumer aspects of the service charge issue, and therefore could not represent the interests of small business at the time. However, as stated in its brief to the committee during the hearing, small business concerns in this area are at least as important for three basic reasons.
First, small businesses typically have less choice in their financial dealings than do customers, since their freedom to switch business relationships with bankers is more restricted than for consumers. Second, the magnitude of service charge costs to small business is proportionately greater, often totalling hundreds of dollars.
Third, unpredictable and sizeable changes in bank service charges can have a dramatic negative impact on the ability of small businesses to plan their operations and cash flow, and could in turn affect the viability of the businesses themselves.
The CFIB asked the Government for something it usually does not ask for, government intervention, so that the Government would uphold for small businesses the measures taken voluntarily by the banks for consumers. The Minister of State for Finance said in his statement on September 15 that he expects increased competition in the financial sector to play a key role in ensuring reasonable service charge practices. Yet the CFIB also argued that any positive benefits from deregulation of financial services have yet to be seen for small businesses. It claims that the most apparent effect of deregulation to date is that the profit margins on big business lending have been narrowed, causing banks to resort to the imposition of larger and more numerous service charges on small businesses. Also, small businesses are captive customers who suffer greatly as a result of such cost saving actions as closing unprofitable bank branches in small towns on which small businesses often depend.
They felt that the effectiveness of voluntary compliance is suspect "in such an unbalanced market context". Their recommendations were as follows. One, complete information regarding current levels of and changes to service charges must be available to small businesses. Two, charge-back fees for NSF cheques must be eliminated for small businesses. Three, annual monitoring of bank practices in the area of small businesses ought to be put in place.

September 29, 1988
Bank Act
The CF1B tried to negotiate better treatment on service charges with the Canadian Bankers' Association but made no headway on the NSF charge-back issue. The Government gave no quarter here either or anywhere else on that issue in its announcement to extend similar disclosure and complaint resolution benefits to businesses.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, here are the Government's measures for small businesses. Consistent with what is now proposed for personal accounts, the amendments to Bill C-140 and the draft regulations will, first, entitle businesses when they open accounts to receive an enhanced disclosure of charges applying and information on the institution's procedures for handling complaints. Second, they will ensure that banks make available to the public for examination, on request, a list of all charges for business services in their branches doing commercial business. Third, they will provide for ongoing disclosure of core account-related business charges through a brochure available to the public. Fourth, they will provide thirty-day pre-notification, through statements, of changes in account-related charges. The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions will also mediate complaints on behalf of small business account holders.
While all of the recommendations of the CFIB were not accepted, the organization is said to be pleased that most of their issues were dealt with. The main concession that small businesses did not achieve is the cancellation of the fee banks charge for depositing an NSF cheque, and God knows they do get them. The Government has promised to monitor the situation. If it does not improve, tougher action supposedly will be taken. We will see.
I and my Party will be watching closely to see if the disclosure of information on financial service charges continues. We will also carefully monitor whether consumers and small businesses are treated with fairness and consideration in the weeks to come. We are dealing here with a very important issue. We are dealing with small businesses which create a very large number of jobs in Canada. It is an appeal to Canadians by the small business community to be sensitive to their needs.
I recommend that the Minister be very open and fair in dealing with this problem.

Mr. Speaker, I was just having an interesting discussion with the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). He was pleading with me to let this wet spaghetti Bill, Bill C-140, pass. He was pleading with me. He was crying. He was saying "Please". This is the man who called me a Johnny-come-lately. I called him a Tommy-come-never.
Oh, oh!

Here he was sitting on my left trying to outflank me on the left and he was appealing. I knew I was on my left because that is where my heart is. The Minister was pleading with me. I could see the tears rolling down his cheeks. He was saying: "Please, please-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I do want people to look closely at me. I am certainly not crying. I am not a very emotional person. I was trying to argue with the Hon. Member that it would be very much in his interests to see this Bill passed today. He disagrees with me, so he does not have to go on with any further theatrics.

Mr. Speaker, folks watching on TV may have seen the Minister on my left and they might have wondered what was happening. Was I surrendering silently to the Tory Juggernaut? The Minister says he is not a very emotional person. But he was crying inside and laughing on the outside.
Oh, oh!

On the tenet of the proposition that he made, he was propositioning me. He was saying to me that half a loaf is better than no loaf. I know that anybody who lays that argument on me has surrendered the basic argument. He said: "Please, half a loaf is better than no loaf. Isn't it better that they get Bill C-140 than nothing at all?"
Let us just see what Bill C-140 says. It reads:
-immediately after Section 202 thereof, the following Sections:
"202.1 A bank shall not open an account in the name of a customer unless, at the time the account is opened, the bank provides the individual who requests the opening of the account with
(a)	a copy of the account agreement signed by that individual:
(b)	information in writing-
(c)	information in writing-
Then it goes on:
(i) any increase to the charges referred to-
Shall be in writing, Mr. Speaker, in subparagraph (d) we find:
(d)	information in writing-
(e)	such other information in writing as is prescribed.
202.2 A bank shall disclose, in the prescribed manner, to its customers and to the public, the charges applicable with respect-
It is more in writing, Mr. Speaker. In writing, in the prescribed form. Then it goes on:
A bank shall not increase any charge applicable to an account with the bank or introduce any new charge applicable to an account with the bank unless the bank discloses such charges in the prescribed manner.. .
Obviously in writing, Mr. Speaker, in triplicate, with the appropriate colours going to the bureaucrats in the Bank of Canada, to the Minister and every other minion around. That is what it says. Then here is the classic in clause 202.4:
September 29, 1988

A bank shall establish procedures for dealing with complaints made by customers of the bank . ..
The bank will start watching itself. It is like putting Count Dracula in charge of the Red Cross blood bank. You put the banks in charge of hearing complaints. It says in here that there will be a local banker who will hear your complaint, and if you are not satisfied the local banker will funnel that up to a regional banker, who will then, if you are not satisfied, funnel it up to a national banker. That is supposed to be an effective system of redress for consumers. Then it goes on to say:
A bank shall file with the Superintendent a copy of its procedures established pursuant to subsection (1).
In the appropriate form, Mr. Speaker. That means in writing, with the appropriate copies to the appropriate minions. Then it says:
A bank shall, in the prescribed manner, provide customers of the bank who have complaints with respect to their accounts with prescribed information on how they may contact the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
So it will be informing them, in the prescribed form, in writing, of course, with the appropriate number of copies to the appropriate minions and on and on. Then you start looking for the meat among all of the potatoes. You cannot find one morsel of meat, not one morsel. This is a deliberate attempt to denude the forests of this country. I can imagine the number of trees it will take to pass all this information in the prescribed form, in writing, with the appropriate copies to the appropriate minions. Give me a break, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister comes over here with his crocodile tears and suggests that I should accept this half a loaf. I would not even call it bread, Mr. Speaker. Man does not live by bread alone. He has to live by some substantive amendments to the Bank Act that give customers of the bank some security with respect to their dealings with the bank. That is what we need, not this Casper Milquetoast Bill. I see it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, the Government's spending spree on energy megaprojects once
again shows the Tories talking one way and acting another. Despite the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) words on the environment, echoed by the Energy and Environment Ministers, it is clear that Tories do not understand that an energy policy is an environmental policy. Look at the record.
In November, 1984, they cut the energy division of the National Research Council, wiping out research on renewable energy, energy conservation and energy alternatives. Clearly the Tories prefer to buy votes through megaprojects. That is their energy policy.
For us, an energy policy is an environmental policy. We are committed to shifting our dependence from non-renewable to renewable energy sources. We must work hard on energy efficiency, aim at a sustainable energy policy, and look beyond the next 40 years instead of the next four.
