speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Attewell (Don Valley East) moved:
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA POST CORPORATION ADVISABILITY OF AMENDING ACT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Canada Post Corporation Act so as to make Canada Post an essential public service which would render illegal any strikes affecting postal delivery.
He said: Mr. Speaker, again I would like to pay a compliment to the whole process of parliamentary reform. It is through that process that individual Members such as myself can speak on some urgent and serious matters. This particular motion was drawn and was subsequently declared a votable motion.
The sending and receiving of mail over the years has played an important, sometimes critical, role in the lives of most Canadians. Prompt, reliable, low-cost service is essential to individuals, especially seniors, and to small and large companies.
As recently as yesterday I visited the Glynnwood Retirement Residence in Thornhill, as well as Thomson Court Apartments in Markham, which is also a retirement home. It was interesting to see how keen the residents were to check their mailboxes. It is not only a matter of anxiety over the
Canada Post
timely receipt of pension cheques but also the receipt of much treasured letters from loved ones and friends.
Canada Post Corporation has the privilege of operating as a monopoly in providing mail service to all Canadians. With this privilege there is an obligation to meet the needs of its customers which comprise the entire population of Canada, including every business and institution in the country. As a result, every day the corporation faces the task of moving 30 million pieces of mail to more than 10 million addresses.
There is no room or time in an operation of this magnitude to cope with interruptions caused by strikes. It is the Canadian people who suffer, the people who must put up with inconveniences, higher costs, and even loss of business, the people who must also subsidize the corporation for its losses through their taxes.
We suffered through three postal strikes in the past year William Johnson stated in the August 25 edition of The Gazette of Montreal: "The third postal strike in 14 months should convince even the most timid: the right to strike is out".
The Canadian people are the ones who bear the heaviest burden and who are made most vulnerable. They must be protected. That is why I have proposed Motion No. 113 which states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the
advisability of amending the Canada Post Corporation Act so as to make
Canada Post an essential public service which would render illegal any strikes
affecting postal delivery.
Constant interruptions in mail service as we have witnessed over the past years can no longer be tolerated. The effects have been devastating. When I speak of devastation I am not simply referring to a case of a Christmas card arriving on the first day of spring, nor an invitation suddenly surfacing after the event in question has taken place. I am talking about the real hardship felt by many senior citizens dependent upon postal delivery for their pension cheques, cheques that provide money for their food, shelter-the necessities of life, not the frills. I am also talking about the ruin of many small businesses whose entire operations depend upon regular mail service. Businesses such as small insurance agencies, publishing houses, and companies engaged in direct marketing through the mails are particularly hard hit by strikes.
Just this afternoon I spoke with Barry Cosburn who is President of the Markham based insurance firm of Cosburn, Griffiths & Branham Insurance Brokers Limited. He said: "Being a business dependent on Canada Post, we view it to be in our best interest to have Canada Post declared an essential service and, as a matter of fact, I would go further and privatize it".
I spoke to another businessman today who shares my concern about Canada Post and who is totally supportive of the motion. Graydon Card is the owner of Card's Home Hardware and Appliances of Stouffville. His comments were as follows:

September 29, 1988
Canada Post
Since over 50 per cent of our daily business volume is done on a credit system, it is mandatory that our receivables come in on a regular and reliable basis.
Past strikes have been so detrimental and threatening to our business, that we had to resort to personally delivering our invoices to over 400 customers.
I talked to another very successful businessman in Markham. Mark Cullen is the General Manager and Vice-President of Weall and Cullen Nurseries Ltd. He expressed his frustrations with Canada Post with the following comments:
We spend about $250,000 in business with Canada Post. I wish I could say it is worth it.
The unions only have to threaten to strike and a lot of damage is done. If we had just mailed a direct response catalogue, the response rate drops drastically since customers are worried that our products, many of which are very seasonal, may not arrive in time.
If they go on strike and we just happen to have 30,000 mailers ready to go, we must throw them out.
The actual strike and threat of strikes can throw our budgets completely out of whack.
Unlike any other supplier, Canada Post's rules are quite rigid. It is cash up front and you must comply with certain packaging and labelling conditions. That would be fine if we had confidence in their ability to deliver our mailings on time.
In closing, Mr. Cullen said:
Canada Post for example had guaranteed a maximum five-day delivery on a mailing of 500,000 catalogues. When we found out that many were not delivered for two and three weeks, we gave the business to a private courier.
Mark Cullen is very supportive of my motion.
Canada Post Corporation has a responsibility to all users. Many businesses have been drawn into bankruptcy as a consequence of strikes. The country simply cannot tolerate the prolonged interruptions of what is in fact an essential service.
Some 80 per cent of the total mail volume handled by Canada Post is contributed by the business community. Is it fair to jeopardize the future of such good customers by disrupting service to them? Is this the way to treat and keep good customers?
Competition for Canada Post is increasing. Private couriers, telephone, telex, expanding communications technology, and facsimile transmissions are all seeking this business. It is more important than ever now that service is not disrupted for any reason.
Parcel mail decreased by 8 per cent in the past year. One must deduce that private couriers are, therefore, providing more reliable service.
The 1981 postal strike is estimated to have caused a loss of $3 billion to Canadian business. Can we allow these types of losses to continue to affect a sector that provides 92 per cent of the job creation in Canada?
Small business is particularly vulnerable to the effects of postal strikes. Many have not been able to survive them, but even for those who have managed to keep their heads above water there has been a high price paid with serious impacts upon their growth and potential future.
Disruption of collections has affected cash flows and delayed receivables have resulted in heavy interest payments. Additional costs to cover alternate services provided by private couriers have been incurred. Inevitable sales drops and staff reductions have frequently resulted in frustration and broken morale that has been difficult to rebuild. It is tough when one has to deal with the consequence of an action but cannot control the cause.
Canada Post was incorporated in the fall of 1981. Now 62,000 people are employed there. It was a series of strikes that denied postal service to Canadians which was a leading factor in Canada Post becoming a Crown corporation, but even this new status has not eliminated the problem of strikes.
Postal strikes provided an opportunity for competition to grow, taking over markets once dominated by Canada Post. Once again, who stands to lose the most? It is the taxpayer.
When Canada Post was incorporated, it faced a deficit of over $300 million and a monumental task to meet financial obligations, to gain operational control of the organization, and to establish a peaceful relationship with the labour force. Factors such as strikes that limit efficient use of the workforce have a significant impact on the cost of providing postal services.
The annual report of Canada Post for 1987-88 says:
Only in an environment where there is a balance between service, efficiency and postal rates can business grow, compete, reach and maintain profitability.
There is no room in this plan for strikes. Moves to improve reliability within Canada Post include the establishment of the Marchment committee in 1985. The first nine recommendations deal with the need for reliable service. The report reads, and I quote:
All Canadians require a postal service. In particular, they require a reliable first and second class mail system ... consistent, dependable, regular, movement of mail.
We know from experience that "consistent, dependable and regular movement of mail" cannot be achieved while an organization is coping with internal management-labour problems that consistently lead to strikes.
Once again, who is the big loser? It is the taxpayer, but it seems that the corporation's future is also being held up for ransom by troubling strikes.
To the credit of Canada Post, it has, indeed, implemented many of the recommendations of the Marchment report. However, it has been an uphill battle that unquestionably has been hindered by continuing labour-management problems, problems that in most instances resulted in strikes for which the Canadian public has had to pay too large a price.
Over the years Canada Post has suffered severe criticism for continually operating with a deficit. Gradually, this deficit is being reduced, from $129 million in 1986-87 to $30 million this year; a significant reduction.
September 29, 1988

However, I believe that most of this progress has been made through increases in postal rates, not improved efficiency.
During the four-year period from 1979 to 1983, the first-class postage rate was increased by the Liberal Government from 17 cents to 32 cents, an 83.7 per cent increase. In the five-year period from 1984 to January of 1989, the Progressive Conservative Government will have increased the rate from 32 cents to 38 cents, which amounts to a 17.9 per cent increase.
In the coming year, Canada Post Corporation is expected to break even for the first time in 20 years. As the plans are implemented there will not only be improved standards of moving mail, but these steps will help to reduce mail handling costs.
We, the customers, stand to benefit from these improvements. Let us not let a labour strike destroy the chance of attaining these goals, for such improvements are not without cost.
We invested $190 million in 1987-88 to support fundamental changes to improve the postal system. During the same period, Canada Post had to cope with three postal strikes and the negative impact that these must have had.
Canadians have been receiving and sending mail since 1705, when Pedro da Silva, Canada's first recorded mail carrier, was commissioned to provide service for both official and private mail between Montreal, Three Rivers, and Quebec City. He had a tough time of it, as the first road connecting these settlements was not opened until 1734, but the mail got through.
Can we allow this important service that has been such an essential part of our lives to be bogged down and rendered ineffective by a never-ending series of strikes?
Labour-management problems of Canada Post have a history of being resolved through strikes, at grievous expense to the Canadian public. The customer, you and I, are the real victims in labour-management feuds for we must pay ever escalating rates and endure poor service. This is a burden we can no longer expect Canadians as individuals or as members of the business community to bear.
It was in 1967 that the Pearson Government legislated employees of the Canada Post Corporation the right to strike. This move has obviously been a mistake.
The Standing Committee on Government Operations, chaired by the Hon. Member from Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann), completed an examination of Canada Post's operational plans last year. On September 22, 1987, it submitted its report and its first recommendation read as follows:
That the Government consider declaring Canada Post an essential service and invoking third party arbitration, if the approach to this year's labour-management negotiations does not reflect the Corporation's crucial importance.
May I stress that that was an all-Party committee that made that recommendation.
Canada Post
In closing, 1 must say that it is now time for this Government to react, I hope in a favourable way to my motion which in part reads as follows:
-consider the advisability of amending the Canada Post Corporation Act so as to make Canada Post an essential public service which would render illegal any strikes affecting postal delivery.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that if you did a Canada-wide survey of Canadians, individuals, and businesses, you would find that a tremendously high rate of concerned Canadians would want to pass my motion if they were indeed here in the House of Commons.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA POST CORPORATION ADVISABILITY OF AMENDING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just have a couple of comments to make because I noticed that some Members want to put their feelings on the record about this particular motion. 1 suppose every word in the motion could be taken literally, such as the word "strike" and the words "any strikes affecting postal delivery". The biggest and most effective strikes affecting postal delivery were struck by the Government of Canada.
They were the ones who decided to close rural post offices. They were the ones who decided not to have weekend pick-ups at red mailboxes in the cities. They were the ones who decided to put in so-called supermailboxes and super-duper mailboxes from one end of Canada to the other, replacing the postmaster or the postmistress in those communities. They were the ones who decided that it was more important to make money in the Post Office than it was to have dependable delivery of mail services. They are the ones who, by their philosophy, would for the sake of breaking even or making money go back to the pony express. They would rather go back to the canoe on the St. Lawrence River. They would rather go back to the dog team up North. At least it would not then be a cost on the public purse.
The mail service is as important as medicare. It is as important as anything that one can think of. It is an essential service, but the Government of Canada does not believe it is an essential service.
The Government has brought in changes since it came into power that will radically change the postal service of Canada, so radically that we will no longer see a post office in a small community in Canada with a flag beside it. That is usually the one federal building in the community, and we are talking about 5,584 communities. There are 5,584 rural post offices, and those post offices are slated to close.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA POST CORPORATION ADVISABILITY OF AMENDING ACT
speechtext: What does that have to do with postal delivery?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA POST CORPORATION ADVISABILITY OF AMENDING ACT
speechtext:
Every one of them is going to close. The Hon. Member over here is asking: "What does that have to do with postal delivery?" I thought that this motion was about postal delivery. He is asking: "What does that have to do with it when somebody can go to the next community, to some box out of doors and pick up their mail, when somebody can drive along the main street?" That is what the hon. gentleman says.

September 29, 1988
Canada Post
It is one thing for people to say: "Here I am in Ottawa, and this business of closing down the Post Office and going to the local drug store is a good idea. I get off work here in Ottawa at 4.30, 5, or 6 p.m., and I am sure of having the mailbox open. I can always go into the drug store and stand behind someone buying toothpaste or toilet tissue and be served by someone. 1 can get my mail then. This is as better service". That is what the people can say here in Ottawa.
Those post offices in rural areas serve the community. They are the place where residents do all their banking. They are the one federal establishment in those communities that has a federal presence and serves a purpose far beyond just picking up mail.
Another thing I do not like about the philosophy of the Government is that that service can be handed over to the local business person in the community. I have often thought about the closure of rural post offices. I know some Members of the House will not understand what 1 am talking about. I sometimes think that a lot of the time they do not understand what I am talking about.
However, someone goes into one of those new outfits arranged by the Government to be placed in rural areas and he is served by the local businessman. Perhaps he owes him money. Perhaps a person is picking up an unemployment insurance cheque, a Canada pension cheque, disability cheque, an old age pension cheque, or welfare cheque; sometimes he owes the businessman money. Some Members might say that there is nothing wrong with that because he is taking the cheque with the one hand and giving it back with the other.
However, I think there is something a little wrong with that; not only that, but if somebody in the community replaces that postmaster or postmistress, namely a local business person who perhaps may not be in that community but in another community. Granted, the mail box or the post office is a place of security, and people have trust in the person who is handling their cheques and their mail.
All I want to point out is that if in the interpretation of "strikes against postal delivery" Canada Post is an essential public service, it certainly is, and the first people who should recognize that are members of the Government of Canada. If they recognized that, they would not be putting in supermailboxes and establishments out of doors where someone who cannot get around very well has to go there in the middle of winter and pick through the snow to pick up his or her mail, compliments of politicians who believe that the Post Office should make money. Those politicians say that because they are drawing a comparison between the United States, Great Britain, and some other countries. This is not Great Britain. One could take Great Britain and put it in part of Canada and lose it. This is not any other country. This is Canada, spread out in large rural areas.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA POST CORPORATION ADVISABILITY OF AMENDING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity given to me to make a few remarks on this subject. I think that the motion before us is very important and I would like to point out that motion M-113 submitted by Mr. Attewell, one of my colleagues, reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the
advisability of amending the Canada Post Corporation Act so as to make
Canada Post an essential public service which would render illegal any strikes
affecting postal delivery.
Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to point out that Canada Post is already an essential service, an essential service for many people. Some people can use other services like Fax, which is a new technology. Some people can use either the postal service provided by Canada Post or the service offered by Purolator or other companies; these people can afford to pay more for this service and thus have other options. But for the elderly, for young people, for people on low incomes, postal service is already essential. It is not necessary to have an Act of Parliament; we do not need legislation establishing that postal service is essential. It is obvious that Canada Post is an essential service for almost everyone. But some people already have alternatives.
The other aspect of this motion is that it would make any strikes illegal... it is the idea behind this motion, the idea of making any strikes illegal. Just imagine! I think that we live in Canada, where people have human rights. I am quite surprised, but I would have thought I was in Poland. Am I in another country now? A country like Poland where the Communist government has already taken away the right to strike and made it illegal? Has such a law, such an approach, worked? Can a government take away people's human rights? Is it possible to make laws? Obviously. But is it possible for dictators to take away people's human rights, to take away their right to work? Mr. Speaker, I am impressed by the Poles, because they have a government that has all the powers, a government that says it represents all the people and that there is no other institution that can represent the people's interests. No church, no labour union, only the Communist Party can represent the people properly.
That is the approach of the Communist Party in Poland and these people have rejected the NDP. There really is a difference because the NDP is a democratic Party. We entertain socialist notions, notions to promote the interests of ordinary people, but in a democratic way, whereas a Communist party is a Party seeking to impose its views on people. They are determined to outlaw strikes and they have legislation which states that there shall be no strikes and no unions. But in the end, when people represent their own interests, they realize that joining forces can be an advantage. When they find out that working together and presenting a united front give them more power they form a union, but a union which the Government does not recognize as such. Still it does not make any difference. Solidarity is a Polish union representing workers, and their Government simply has to admit the fact and negotiate with these people in a country where dictature prevails.
September 29, 1988

As 1 see it, Mr. Speaker, the emphasis in this motion should be on the words "the Government should consider the advisability of amending the . . . Act". The key word here is "consider". We are simply asking that the proposition be studied.
1 take this opportunity to deal with the motion by saying that some countries have tried to outlaw any attempt by people to be represented. It does not work out because people know that when a Government ignores their interests they have to get together and tell the Government that they expect their interests to be properly represented.
1 would also point out that unions are legal in North America and that strikes were legalized in the 1930s after a number of violent strikes. At the time the American Government thought it would be well advised to acknowledge the existence of union activities through legislation to settle the issue rather than pretend they did not exist and choose to let them take place in illegality.
Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say that the motion must be seriously considered. I would be quite surprised if the Government were to let it come to a vote. I imagine that Government Members will want to talk it out. It is because the concept here . . .

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA POST CORPORATION ADVISABILITY OF AMENDING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the Hon. Member who just spoke on his efforts to make an excellent speech in French. He is to be commended.
It is time we had an election, Mr. Speaker, because I am starting to realize I don't agree with anyone. I don't agree with the motion as proposed because, Mr. Speaker, I do not think we should take away a right of association or a democratic right or a right to strike. I don't agree with my Liberal friend who spoke earlier, trivializing postal services as they are today . . . It's not true that we always go and pick up our mail at a private post office and that we buy stamps next to the toilet paper display. They can go on all they like about the privatization of our postal services, but 1 suggest they look at the polls which clearly show that generally, people are very satisfied with the new system.
Of course, 1 do not agree with the Hon. Member across the way when he says that Canada Post is an essential service. To
Canada Post
a certain extent, it may be essential, and the usual example is that of the elderly who get their pension cheques in the mail and people who get their unemployment insurance cheques. As far as that goes, I agree. But it seems to me that the federal Government, and we have been here for four years, should concentrate on introducing a direct deposit system so that in many cases we could avoid a system that may be disrupted as a result of people exercising their democratic rights.
Mr. Speaker, the Government remains entirely faithful, and I fully subscribe, to the principle of free collective bargaining and the rights it confers, including the right to strike and the right to lock out, throughout the system. Part V of the Canada Labour Code provides a framework of rights and responsibilities designed to promote stable industrial relations between employers and unions in federally-regulated industries, which includes the Canada Post Corporation. Although the responsibility for collective bargaining lies first and foremost with the parties themselves, the Canada Labour Code provides for the assistance of experts in conciliation and mediation cases, where assistance is made available to employees and management when the parties are unable to reach an agreement.
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that collective bargaining in federally-regulated industries is usually a very peaceful process, since about 90 per cent of labour disputes at the federal level are resolved without strikes or lock-outs. Of course, the cases we hear about are the more spectacular ones, and we have two Crown Corporations where that is the case at the present time. Granted, all is not sweetness and light, but 90 per cent of the disputes are settled without strikes or lock-outs.
The right to strike or to impose a lock-out is fundamental to the collective bargaining process in Canada. The possibility of a work stoppage is the final test, and should always be seen as such, for the bargaining mechanism and the economic resources of unions and employers. The same applies to lockouts and the right to lock out should also be considered in that light. Although in most cases, neither party resorts to these measures, without that possibility, serious negotiations would be impossible. In fact, there are labour relations experts who maintain that a work stoppage, in addition to settling a dispute in no uncertain terms, has the effect of clarifying the issues and re-establishing priorities. I must say 1 agree.
The motion before the House today, Mr. Speaker, is flawed in that it proposes to take away the right to strike from employees who lawfully acquired that right. It does not, however, provide any substitute procedures for resolving the dispute. Most of the time, proposals put forward in this House and elsewhere insist on permanent and general compulsory arbitration as the most efficient means to resolve conflicts arising from employment.

September 29, 1988
Canada Post
Mr. Speaker, arbitration plays indeed and important and legitimate role in the collective bargaining process in Canada. First of all, it is clearly mentioned in the Canada Labour Code in connection with the resolution of conflicts which occur during the life of a collective agreement concerning the approval and interpretation of the clauses of negotiated contracts. Moreover, under special circumstances, when every aspect of a situation requires it, Parliament will insist on compulsory arbitration to deal with unresolved issues. However, as a rule, compulsory arbitration has been turned down by the Canadian Government as a favoured model for dispute resolution.
The compulsory arbitration system has never been effective as a means to prevent strikes in countries which have implemented it. Australia is a case in point. In 1904, Mr. Speaker, this country adopted the Commonwealth Conciliation and Arbitration Act which absolutely forbade strikes and lock-outs. That was in 1904. Those who had drafted it felt that compulsory arbitration would replace the more violent process of strikes and lock-outs. Nevertheless, the labour movement in Australia has never really accepted to be deprived of its right to strike.
In 1979, 75 years later, the Australian Minister responsible for Labour Relations made the following comments concerning working relations in Australia during the 1920's:
The experience of the decade would be useful even if showed only one thing, namely, that the Government cannot prevent strikes by legally banning them. In a democracy, people cannot be forced to work if they do not want to-until 1930, strikes were made absolutely illegal under the Conciliation and Arbitration Act. Well, there were more strikes during that period than at any other period in the history of Australia.
That is a glaring example. For that matter, I remember that in the 1960's, Premier Lesage of Quebec had said: "The Queen does not negotiate with her subjects". The funny thing is that not long after that, they all sat together at the same negotiating table. The world has changed, Mr. Speaker!
Under the same law, in the 1930s and subsequent years, Australia experienced over half a century of legislative amendments to recognize the fact that compulsory arbitration is no solution to a conflict on working conditions.
In 1930, barely 20 years later, the total ban on striking in the Australian civil service was cancelled. They then relied a lot more on the criminal provisions of the legislation, together with the required qualifications and enforcement conditions. In addition, strikes and lockouts likely to disrupt interstate trade could result in criminal proceedings. In the late 1960's, Mr. Speaker, since the unions refused to pay their fines, the penalty system collapsed. That led to a review of the procedures used in contempt of court cases. Now, whenever a contract clause is violated, the parties get a second chance. They can still resort to conciliation and arbitration procedures before the criminal provisions of the law are enforced.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that my time is very limited. But the Australian experience proves at least one thing: it is not by passing legislation forbidding strikes or lockouts or by imposing heavy penalties that we can solve the conflict. Since I was a personnel director for quite a while, I sat at a provincial negotiation table. I was totally against imposing penalties of $60,000 a day to a union leader. It just can't be done, it is not realistic, Mr. Speaker, and we must make changes to this Bill.
I congratulate my colleague for his courage in putting it forward but, Mr. Speaker, I think we can find another solution to the problem.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA POST CORPORATION ADVISABILITY OF AMENDING ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today is of the utmost importance for the collective bargaining system. We must therefore ask ourselves which factors must be taken into account in relation to it.
Mr. Speaker, we have had several similar motions in the past. We have also had calls from various quarters for a complete overhaul of our collective bargaining system. We keep receiving recommendations from well-intentioned people asking us to change our industrial relations system and to eliminate strikes and lock-outs.
Mr. Speaker, I say these people are "well-intentioned" because they usually have in mind the impact work stoppages have on innocent people who can do nothing about labour conflicts which affect them. Although well-intentioned, these people generally ignore the complexity of labour conflicts and the importance of industrial relations practices, including to right to resort to economic sanctions which have been worked out through many decades of experience in Canada and in other large industrialized democracies.
We have, in Canada, one of the most refined systems which allows employers and unions to settle their differences, a system which is the envy of many countries in the world. Our collective bargaining system gives employers and unions complete freedom to settle their disputes through direct negotiations without government intervention. In some countries, the parties do not even have this fundamental freedom.
The conciliation and mediation provisions allow employers and unions subject to Part V of the Canada Labour Code to start direct negociations when a deadlock has been reached in the collective bargaining process. If the dispute is not settled by conciliation or mediation, the legislation allows the parties, under certain conditions, to go on strike or to declare a lockout in order to convince the other party that they will not back down from their position in the collective bargaining process. In most cases, Mr. Speaker, the threat of economic sanctions in the final stages of the process is enough to bring about the necessary concessions for a peaceful settlement.
September 29, 1988

The system set up under Part V of the Canada Labour Code ensures the implementation of collective agreements and provides for comprehensive measures to facilitate the collective bargaining process. When I look at the dispute settlement provisions in the Code, 1 am surprised to see how flexible they are and how they apply to a variety of circumstances related to collective bargaining.
One cannot expect a single policy or procedure to solve all social conflicts, but the flexibility of the Canada Labour Code leads me to think very highly of the dispute settlement method established over the years. I believe that the code is flexible enough to make a good dispute settlement mechanism work.
In short, Mr. Speaker, the right to strike or to lock-out can only be acquired seven days after the Minister has exercised an option in the area of conciliation under the Canada Labour Code. Also, pursuant to section 195 of the Labour Code, the Minister can at any time appoint a mediator to help the parties settle their differences. Under section 171 of the code, before the conciliation commissioner or the conciliation office present their reports, the parties can at any time agree in writing that the recommendations are binding. Thus, under these provisions, employers and unions can have access to all conciliation and mediation services which can help them reach a settlement and have the freedom to voluntarily settle the dispute by agreeing in advance to the recommendations made by the conciliation commissioner or conciliation office.
Mr. Speaker, I have explained in general terms the main elements of the collective bargaining process as described in the Canada Labour Code.
In the case of organizations under federal jurisdiction, I should like to make two comments. First of all, under the Labour Code, both management and unions are free to negotiate collective contracts which, in their opinion, are best suited to the conditions of the business, to the priorities and economic constraints facing the industry. When a third party intervenes as a conciliator or mediator, the parties involved determine the rules within the framework of collective bargaining, and conduct their own negotiations, the third party remaining impartial and helping them define the parameters of the matters in dispute, identify areas where compromises are possible and find ways of getting out of a deadlock.
Mr. Speaker, this approach is quite similar to that which the Government has adopted in many other areas of our social and economic life. Much more than in the past, the Government has encouraged the private sector to show leadership and rely a lot less on the Government to widen its economic outlook. Workers and businessmen therefore must assume greater responsibilities and seize every opportunity for growth.
From the labour relations point of you, Mr. Speaker, this means that management and unions will have more and more to solve their differences without Government's intervention. The conciliation and mediation processes provided for under
Canada Post
the Canada Labour Code are based on this approach by which the responsibility for negotiations and dispute settlements falls first and foremost on the interested parties. Part V of the Canada Labour Code defines the rights and responsibilities of both management and unions and clearly indicates that the parties involved in collective bargaining must find a way to settle their disputes.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize the fact that the parties must deal dutifully with the collective bargaining process and understand that any reluctance on their part to reach a negotiated settlement, undermines a system aimed at encouraging constructive collective bargaining. We have witnessed before situations where both management and unions had relinquished their responsibilities for the settlement of a dispute to a third party, including public authorities.
Mr. Speaker, we must curb Governments overwelming tendency to interfere with our lives. The Government's reluctance to adopt a legislation to force workers back to work, except in cases where conflicts could jeopardize Canada's interests, clearly demonstrate its intention to encourage both management and unions to solve their own conflicts by themselves. That is why I fail to see the need for such a motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to participate in this debate this afternoon in the final leg of of the Thirty-third Parliament. It may be very historic. My colleague from Don Valley East and I will be back here for the Thirty-fourth Parliament to look at some other legislation. It has been a long four years, and we look forward to the fall and the pending election.
My colleague from Winnipeg North Centre spent some time on the committee reviewing some of the postal concerns. I want to say at this time that I would like to thank all the participants who looked into what were at times some very trying times for the postal corporation. I think we have drawn very positive conclusions and made changes that have really worked quite well.
Despite some of the strikes that have occurred, to which my colleague from Don Valley East referred, in fact the Canada Post Corporation, for the first time in many, many years, is showing a ledger that is more acceptable to Canadians. This is despite the fact that there have been some very difficult strikes. I, like the Hon. Member, have considered naming Canada Post Corporation an essential service. 1 think Canadians as a whole believe that this may be a route the Government should look at. However, we have to be cautious before we automatically consider making such a major move. We should consider especially the immediate impact it would have on the relationship between the-

Adjournment Debate

speechtext:
That's right, between the Crown corporation and the labour movement.
Let me mention something in defence of one of the unions, the rural postmasters' union. Its members have never been on strike and in fact, in most cases they have acted very congenially and have worked hard to find solutions, although we are now entering a phase of change in rural post offices.
The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) thought that change was a negative idea. I suspect that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) did as well. The facts are starting to bear us out. Even with this change, we have made tremendous progress, despite the Rural Dignity organization preaching gloom and doom and saying that Canadians are getting less service. Over the countless months and days we have debated the postal changes, in fact they have have worked amazingly well with very little disruption in postal service.
In my own community, for example, a change that took place was reported by a local paper. A retail post office won unanimous consent. I along with the entire community looked at the change and the community in fact totally agreed to put the post office into a franchise store. In fact, today, the mail is available nine to ten hours a day, six days a week, and that is what the community wanted and agreed upon. The argument that change would affect us in such a negative way more than likely is proving to be false all over Canada.
I mentioned the fact that the Post Office is now in a very positive way in terms of balancing its budget. In fact, it is returning to Canadian users some of this funding by no longer charging for post boxes, something which was done on an ad hoc basis.
I think that my colleague for Winnipeg North Centre will agree that should the Post Office become a little more efficient, some of the lower costs to the Canadian taxpayers will in fact be turned back to the users. That is what I think is good management by the Post Office.
Should the time come that postal strikes become as violent and disruptive as they seem to tend to want to become, for no reason at all, we did make a recommendation. Just recently, we had the threat of a postal strike. There was a short strike. They were asking for payment for their lunch leave while most of these people are paid an average of $25 a hour. I think it was demonstrated that the Crown corporation would not tolerate that, and in fact there was a resolution to the strike.
1 notice that my time is almost up. When the strikes were going on, the Post Office somehow managed to get most of the mail through. I think that is completely different from having a postal strike that totally disrupts services, as has happened in certain instances.
At this time I would also like to thank my colleague from Nanaimo-Alberni who yielded his position this evening to someone who knew better how to speak on this matter. As a result, I would like to commend him.

REQUEST FOR FEDERAL FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE/MINISTER'S POSITION

Mr. Speaker, the topic tonight is again the environment and the question of whether or not Canadians are entitled to know about the quality of water they have to look forward to for this and future generations. Canadians would like to believe a Prime Minister no matter who that person happens to be because the environment is too important to be left to rhetoric. However, the gap between rhetoric and fact is so wide it now requires an explanation. There must be an explanation about an issue that has been raised in this House many, many times, most recently on September 16 of this year.
Canadians are entitled to have an explanation from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). They are entitled to know whether the Prime Minister's sudden interest in the environment is driven by polls or by a genuine interest and desire to change the alarming trends we are witnessing, particularly in relation to surface and ground water. Therefore, the issue is very simply whether or not Canadians will have clean water. It is a question of recreation and of general ecological well-being. It is an issue in which this federal Government has a role to play.
The history is very simple. It is important that we remind the Government that in the 1960s and 1970s some $2 billion was spent by Ottawa under the National Housing Act by way of loans and grants to some 1,500 municipalities to build, repair, and improve sewers or to build sewage treatment plants and the like. A further $400 million was spent in the early 1980s but not by this Government. We notice, particularly in the last few months running up to the election, that this Government has made major commitments to the tune of over $12 billion, without counting the nuclear submarines. It is a commitment which probably keeps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) awake at night wondering how he will ever pay for all these promises. Out of that $12 billion, not one penny is being committed in response to a request made frequently by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities which calls for a $15 billion joint program by all three levels of government to rebuild our sewers and protect water quality.
September 29, 1988

The Liberal Party, as you know, Mr. Speaker, in 1986 and again last year, committed itself to providing the federal share of almost $5 billion for this type of participation. We want to get some information from the Tories. Do they really believe in water quality and health and recreation along our rivers and lakes? We want to know what the Conservative's environmental vision is all about. Is the Tory environmental vision driven by their reading of public opinion polls? Is it driven by conviction? Is it driven by the inevitable realization that we have to change our ways, our trends, and even our values if we are to survive as a species on this planet? Or, is it because the backroom boys are saying it is good public relations because the polls seem to say there is a big environment vote out there that must be grabbed while it lasts in order to win the election?
Despite all this we want to take the Prime Minister seriously. This is why we in the Official Opposition are pressing him here again tonight, perhaps the last night before an election is called. We are pressing him to live up to his statement on the environment to show Canadians that he means what he says; that water will be protected, that rivers and lakes will be clean again; that beaches will be open to the public. That is what we expect the Parliamentary Secretary to confirm in the name of his Prime Minister if the Prime Minister of Canada wants to retain his credibility.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has questioned the priority which the federal Government assigns to water quality and whether we will be participating in the Government of Ontario's Lifelines Program.
Let me deal with this latter aspect first. We have had the opportunity to review the details of the Lifelines Program which is to assist Ontario municipalities in the refurbishment of their water and sewage systems.
Municipal infrastructure is clearly an area of provincial and municipal responsibility. The federal Government cannot assist in programs such as these for reasons which have previously been made clear to this House. 1 am pleased that the Government of Ontario has designed a provincial program responsive to that province's needs and has taken this initiative without federal assistance.
This is not to say that the federal Government is not concerned about water quality or is not active in the area of water policy. In November, 1987, the Government announced its federal water policy. The over-all objective of the policy is to encourage the use of fresh water in an efficient and equitable manner consistent with the social, economic, and environmental needs of present and future generations.
The policy maps out five basic courses of action; fair and realistic water pricing based on consumption, federal leadership in water science, an integrated approach to water resource planning involving all sectors of society, a broad review of
Adjournment Debate
water legislation, and a public awareness program on water issues.
We already devote more than $300 million annually to encourage and improve the quality of water in Canada. In areas which are clearly a federal responsibility, such as the research, development, and transfer of new waste water technologies, the co-ordination of action among provinces, and dealing with international boundary issues, we have accepted our responsibilities and delivered on our commitments.
For example, we are already participating with Ontario to improve the quality of water in the Great Lakes. In 1987, we signed a protocol to the Canada-U.S. Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement committing both countries to clean up areas of environmental concern. In June, 1988, the Government announced its $110 million action plan to protect, conserve, and restore the St. Lawrence River.
In short, the federal Government clearly recognizes its responsibility in the area of water policy and continues to assign the highest priority to the protection of this most valuable of natural resources, water.
IMMIGRATION-LOCATION OF OFFICE IN MINISTER'S RIDING/COST OF RELOCATING OFFICE

Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of raising in this Chamber at this time a question that I posed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) on September 21 of this year, concerning an issue that I thought was very embarrassing to the Minister personally and very embarrassing to the Government. I thought the Minister lacked any credibility whatsoever in terms of her response to my question.
Essentially the issue was the relocation of a new immigration office in the heart of her riding in St. Paul's, Toronto. By way of background, the Minister closed the immigration office at 230 Bloor Street in Toronto and relocated that office in the heart of her own community for obvious political gains. All through that the Minister said, "Well, I didn't know", which says one of two things: first, the Minister does not know about the operation of her own Department in relocating an office in her own backyard, or she was not exactly forthcoming with Members in this Chamber.
Because there were the long line-ups that we witness in centres right across Metropolitan Toronto and other centres as a result of the mismanagement of the Government vis-a-vis immigration and refugee policy, at the first sight of a problem what did the Minister do? She simply airlifted the office, removed the staff and materials again, and went to 4900 Yonge Street. All this cost the taxpayers of Canada $30,000 for moving from Bloor Street to her own office on Eglinton Avenue in her riding. Another $30,000 was spent moving from that office to the one at 4900 Yonge Street. More important, the lease for the office in her own riding was for $600,000 for five years which comes to a total cost of $3 million, plus the $60,000.

September 29, 1988
Adjournment Debate
In order to save face the Minister created a need in order to keep that office running, not for immigration purposes but for training programs. I was somewhat offended, as were most other Canadians who are involved with this issue, because the office was moved for obvious politically appetizing reasons. Those reasons quickly went sour. At the first sight of them going sour the Minister did not delay and moved her offices yet again.
This is a colossal abuse of one's national responsibilities for a Department of Government and was carried out for purely personal, political, partisan gains that the Minister would make in her own riding. The Minister suggested in the House that the reason she moved the office-after saying she did not know it was going into her riding-was that the facilities were wrong, that they were located in the wrong building, that there were not enough waiting rooms, washrooms, and other facilities to handle that type of caseload. She happens to be the Minister of a Department. If in fact she says that it was the wrong place because there were not the proper facilities, then why as the Minister did she allow her Department to go through with the various relocations? It is very obvious that she wanted to display the ability to be able to move an office in her riding, went through with it despite the fact that the facilities were not right, only to have the community complain about it. She then reacted and moved it to 4900 Yonge Street.
I have been speaking to officers at 4900 Yonge Street. Not only do they not have the facilities there to handle the type of caseload that they expect, but the employment officers have been informed by their superiors that they will now have to relocate and move out of the location in order to satisfy the need that they anticipate for the immigration work.
Outside providing business and work for those in the moving industry, what is being accomplished by this Minister of Immigration? If she thought that it was not the proper place, then she could have stopped the move. If she thought that it was the wrong place but wanted to move for political reasons, then she should admit it. If she wants to solve the problems of line-ups, I suggest that she should look beyond her own riding and her own backyard. Not only should she try to solve the line-ups there, but she should try to solve them at the Bloor and Islington office where my constituents have to line up beginning at four and five in the morning.
If she were courageous and forthright enough to deal with the refugee backlog, then maybe those line-ups would be getting smaller. If we had on the job management those lineups would not be there. Instead of dealing with immigrants by allowing them to line up at four and five in the morning like cattle, they should be given appropriate meeting times for scheduling appointments, as is done in every other office. I do not see why the immigration office operation should be an exception.
These are the questions which remain unanswered. Why did the Minister move the office into her riding in the first place if she knew that the facilities were wrong? Why does she
continue to waste taxpayers' dollars for her own political benefit? Instead of only looking after her own political backyard, as Minister responsible for a national Department why does she not show some concern for the other line-ups that we see right across the country, not only across Metropolitan Toronto? If she has an answer to the refugee backlog and provides it before the election, as any courageous Minister of the Crown would do, then those line-ups might get smaller.
I look forward to the Parliamentary Secretary providing some of the answers that obviously the Minister, unfortunately, did not provide back on September 21.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate and respond to the question. In a way it shows that I agree with my colleague opposite. One has to be on one's toes concerning the administrative decisions made at various government levels. I can tell you that it is not necessarily a soft job to be given a Department these days because, when you get a Department you become more visible, but to the detriment of your family, your friends, your riding. It would almost be better if nothing ever happened any more in your riding, no family problems, no arguments with your friends. A moment ago my colleague took us to task about the refugee backlog. We have nothing to learn from them. For months on end, in cahoots with the Liberal Senators in the other place, they did everything they could to thwart our attempts to find a fair and equitable solution to a problem which had lasted for much too long already.
Mr. Speaker, this gives me an opportunity to set the record straight and describe the series of events. We began to review the situation in early 1988. The Minister did not hold the employment and immigration portfolio at the time. We examined the situation and when we checked the location of the famous... on Yonge Street, it was inadequate. So we asked ourselves where was our clientele for this immigration service and we came to the conclusion that it was in two very specific regions of Toronto, namely Scarborough and North York. There it is, we said. So they made an offer to Treasury Board to go in the region of Scarborough and in the region of North York. So they commented on that and decided to locate in a commercial zone in those two areas. And accordingly the Treasury Board said yes, etc. So, away they go from Yonge Street and along their way. Except that, and this caused the problem, there was indeed an administrative error, not an error in . .. Instead of choosing North York, they went to North Toronto. Something quite different! They went to North Toronto, indeed in the constituency of the Minister who later became the Minister of Employment and Immigration, which she was not then, a residential area. It was quite out of place. There was no way they could remain there.
September 29, 1988

And they did not... they started all over again and will locate elsewhere-in fact one is in Scarborough, and the other will be in North Toronto. Now, my colleague opposite says there was an unneeded expenditure on relocation costs and the lease that will be needed in the North Toronto. No. Because that is a residential area that is entitled to some services, that centre becomes the training centre for all employees. So, it will be used. We will honour our lease and it will be more in line with the area's zoning. The one in Scarborough already is in a commercial area, the one in North York will also be in a commercial area.
And, Mr. Speaker, until the North York office opens, because there are waiting lists, indeed, because the refugee problem was not solved in time, the Hon. Minister gave
Adjournment debate
instructions for the office to remain open 24 hours a day to give better service and eliminate the backlog. From 4 a.m. people wait at the door in order to be heard.
So, Mr. Speaker, there you have the answers to the question, and I am pleased I will probably be the last speaker to rise before elections are called, if only this can be done before 10 a.m. tomorrow!
